replies: Trainee, your career agent — I save and use details you give to find jobs, tailor applications and prep interviews. I saved: Knows SQL, Excel and Tableau; 2 years of reporting experience. Is that right?

Key skills you already have that match a data analyst role
- SQL — core for querying databases, joins, aggregations and building datasets.
- Excel — essential for ad-hoc analysis, pivot tables, VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP, modeling and quick data cleanup.
- Tableau — relevant for dashboards, visualization, and communicating findings to stakeholders.
- 2 years of reporting experience — shows domain experience producing regular analyses, meeting deadlines, and working with business users (valuable for product/operations/finance analyst roles).
Gaps many data analyst postings also ask for (so you can close them)
- A programming language for analysis (Python or R) — useful for advanced analytics, automation and reproducible workflows.
- Statistical or A/B testing knowledge — basics of hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, experiment design.
- SQL depth examples — window functions, performance tuning, complex CTEs — show these on your resume if you can.
- Data engineering basics — familiarity with ETL, data pipelines, and databases (Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake) often preferred.
- Business-context metrics — experience defining KPIs, building reports that drove decisions, and measuring impact with numbers.
One next step: tell me which exact data analyst jobs you want (industry and city or remote) and I’ll search for role matches and tailor which of your skills to highlight. Is that the direction you want?

replies:
Quick targeted prep for a final-round analyst interview at Lincoln International — what to do now, what they’ll assess, a 10-step plan, likely questions (behavioral, technical, case/fit), two concise sample answers you can adapt, and one practice prompt to start now.
What they’ll assess (short)
- Fit for mid‑market M&A boutique work: commercial curiosity, client instincts, stamina for execution.  
- Technical fundamentals: accounting, three-statement linkage, basic modeling and valuation (DCF, comps, precedent transactions).  
- Deal judgment: ability to frame a valuation/structuring question, trade-offs, and recommendations.  
- Communication and presence: concise structure, defendable reasoning, clear recommendations.  
- Teamwork and coachability: examples showing you take direction, correct errors, and deliver under pressure.
10-step prep plan (do these in order)
1) Confirm logistics and format (who interviews you, panel or one-on-one, length, whether there’s a modeling test). If you don’t know, get that now — I’ll tailor after you share it.
2) One-page cheat sheet: concise bullets for accounting links, WACC formula and components, DCF steps, when to use exit multiple vs. Gordon growth, and common multiple ranges by sector you expect. Keep it to one page for quick review.
3) Rehearse accounting → cash flow: be able to explain in 60s how net income becomes cash from operations and why EBITDA ≠ cash flow (working capital, non‑cash items, capex).
4) Walk through a DCF aloud (60–90s): project FCFs, discount with WACC, compute terminal value, sum → EV → subtract net debt → equity value → per‑share. Include sensitivity drivers.
5) Read any publicly available Lincoln deals you know and prepare 2 reasons you want Lincoln specifically (mid‑market deal exposure; hands‑on modeling & client contact; sector focus you can point to). If you can’t fetch deal lists now, state the types of deals you want to work on and why.
6) Prepare 4–6 STAR stories mapped to core competencies: teamwork, ownership, handling pressure, correcting mistakes, learning quickly. Keep each 40–60s and include a result (metric if possible).
7) “Walk me through your resume” practice (60–90s): lead with analytical accomplishments and transaction-related outcomes; end with why analyst at Lincoln.
8) Run 3 technical drills and 3 short case drills aloud (timed). Focus on clarity and stepwise logic, not finishing every calculation.
9) Prepare 3 thoughtful questions to ask each interviewer (deal-specific, team structure, how performance is measured, typical analyst path).
10) One hour before the interview: 15m accounting drills, 15m valuation formulas, 15m read STAR bullets, 15m mental warm-up + logistics check.
Likely questions and how to structure answers
Behavioral (STAR)
- Tell me about a time you worked on a tight-deadline team.  
- Describe a time you found an error in your analysis and what you did.  
- Give an example when you persuaded someone with data.

Technical
- Walk me through a DCF. (Structure: objective → forecast FCF drivers → discount rate/WACC components → terminal value choice → convert EV to equity value → sensitivity.)  
- How do you calculate WACC? (Cost of equity via CAPM; cost of debt after tax; weights by market value.)  
- How does an increase in capex affect valuation if EBITDA grows? (Explain impact on free cash flow and terminal value; show sensitivity thinking.)
Case / deal-style prompts
- Valuation mini: given revenue, margin and comps, outline approaches (comps, DCF, precedent transactions), state key assumptions, and run a back‑of‑envelope multiple or sensitivity.  
- Structuring advice: founder wants max cash but remains upside — discuss asset vs. share sale, earnouts, rollover equity; weigh tax, liability and buyer preference.
Two concise sample answers to adapt
- Walk me through your resume (90s)
"I began at [Role] at [Company], where I built financial models and supported two transactions, including a [brief measurable outcome — e.g., 1: helped model a $X sale or improved forecast accuracy by Y%]. I then led [project] that improved [metric]. Most recently I [relevant project], which taught me to translate detailed modeling into clear recommendations. I want an analyst role at Lincoln because of its mid‑market focus and opportunity to work directly on deal execution and client-facing analysis from day one."  
(Replace bracketed items with specifics and a metric.)
- Behavioral: correcting an error (45s)
"Situation: I prepared a monthly forecast and missed a deferred revenue adjustment. Task: Correct the forecast before a client review. Action: I traced the source, corrected the model, added an audit tab and peer‑check step. Result: The corrected deck went to the client on time and the new checks reduced similar errors going forward."
One short 3‑part practice exercise now (do one; I’ll score and give a fix)
Pick one and answer in 40–60 seconds:
A) Behavioral: Tell me about a time you made a mistake on a quantitative task. What happened and what did you change?  
B) Technical: How do you go from revenue to unlevered free cash flow? List the line items and why they move.  
Comps trade 7–9x EBITDA. Buyer can improve margins to 25% in 2 years. How would you value it and what sensitivity would you run?  
Say which you choose and give your 40–60s answer; I’ll score structure, evidence and specificity and give one concrete improvement, then the next prompt.
One next step
Tell me which practice prompt (A, B or C) and post your 40–60s answer now.

If you give me a posting, I will prepare an application card for your approval. Here is exactly what I will put on that card, field by field, and where each value comes from or what I'll ask you to provide when it's needed:

1) Employer (company)
- What I'll show: the company name exactly as the job posting states it.
- Source: copied verbatim from the posting. You do not enter this.
2) Role (job title)
- What I'll show: the job title exactly as the posting uses it.
- Source: copied from the posting.

3) Location / place
- What I'll show: city, remote/on-site/hybrid and any site details exactly as the posting lists them.
- Source: posting text.

4) Job link / job identifier
- What I'll show: the job link exactly as returned by the posting source (or the internal job id if the source uses one).
- Source: posting metadata.

5) Pay
- What I'll show: the pay or salary range exactly as the posting lists it, or "not listed" when the posting gives no pay.
- Source: posting.
6) Resume to use (which file)
- What I'll show: options of any confirmed resume(s) you have on file plus a "base" resume option.
- If you have no confirmed resume, the card will prompt you to paste a resume or to type the name and email for the resume header so I can create a base resume.
- What I need from you now if none exist: paste the resume or give name and email for the resume header.

7) Cover letter / short message (optional)
- What I'll create: a ≤120-word cover note draft tailored to the posting, using only your confirmed facts; missing specifics will remain in [brackets] for you to fill.
- What you'll do: review and edit on the card. I will not send it without your approval.
8) Screening questions / application answers
- What I'll show: the exact screening questions from the posting.
- What I'll draft: suggested answers based solely on your confirmed facts; where I lack facts I leave [brackets] or blanks for you to complete.
- You must fill/approve each answer before submission.

9) Attachments
- What I'll include: the selected resume PDF and any other attachments you supply (portfolio, transcripts).
- If you don't supply additional attachments now, those fields remain empty on the card.
10) Work authorization / visa status
- What I'll show: a field for you to type your exact words on work authorization (e.g., "US citizen", "H-1B sponsorship required", "eligible to work in US until MM/YYYY").
- I will not guess or fill this; you type it on the card.

11) Earliest start date / notice period
- What I'll show: a field for your answer (e.g., "two weeks after offer" or "available immediately").
- You type it; I won't invent one.

12) Salary expectation (if asked)
- What I'll show: a field where you can enter a number or range, or leave blank.
- I will not invent salary expectations. If the posting lists a range, I can use that verbatim if you want.
13) Phone / contact on resume
- What I'll show: the contact exactly as you've saved for your resume (name, email, phone).
- If none is saved, the card will prompt: "What name and email should go at the top of your resume?"

14) Questions for the employer / interview availability
- What I'll show: optional free-text fields for you to enter your own questions and your availability.
- I will not add availability without your words.
15) Submission checklist & blocks
- What I'll show: a computed list of what is missing before submission for this posting (for example: resume missing, cover note not approved, screening questions unanswered, work authorization missing, email not connected if the posting requires email).
- This checklist prevents sending until every required item is filled and you approve.

16) What will be sent and to whom
- What I'll show: an explicit statement like: "This application will send: [Resume.pdf], [Cover note], [Screening answers] to [employer's apply endpoint or email]" using exact posting target info.
- You will review this and must approve before anything is sent.
17) Notes / customization I applied
- What I'll show: the tailoring steps I did (keywords emphasized, reordered skills or bullets) and any placeholders left in [brackets].
- This tells you what changed from your resume.

18) Privacy & delivery confirmation
- What I'll show: whether the application sends via the employer portal or by email, and whether your Gmail connection is required to send mail. If your email is not connected and the posting requires email, the checklist will show that as a block.

19) Final approve / send button
- What I'll show: a final approval control you press. I will not send anything without that explicit approval.
What I will not do on the card
- I will not invent or confirm facts about you (experience, dates, titles, authorization). Missing items stay as [brackets].
- I will not submit anything until you press approve on the card.
- I will not connect or read your email unless you explicitly enable that connection.
